summary: For ages 7-8 (with teacher support): make sense of multi-step problems within 1000 by breaking them into ordered sub-problems, choosing and sequencing strategies, estimating a reasonableness benchmark first, and checking with an inverse operation or a different method — revising when the two disagree. The central aim is to replace the keyword habit (tying a word to an operation), which research on released items reports succeeds on under 50% of single-step and under 10% of multi-step problems, with attention to problem structure, and to counter the compulsion to calculate (answering with no estimate and no check). Self-questioning aloud and visual representations (e.g. bar/strip diagrams and number lines for sequencing jumps) are the two levers cited with strong evidence in the WWC grades 4-8 guide; strategy-switching when the first approach stalls should be normalised.
misconceptions: Keyword strategy on multi-step problems — tying a word to an operation and applying operations in the wrong order
Computing an answer with no estimate and no check, accepting answers that are wildly off (compulsion to calculate)
Believing that if the first method doesn't work, you're simply stuck (no strategy-switching)
Doing the sub-steps but not connecting them — losing track of what has been found and what remains

activities.title: Estimate-first multi-step solver with inverse check
steps: Take a two-step problem, e.g. 'A shop had 320 pencils. It sold 4 boxes of 50. How many pencils are left?' and arrange it as two connected sub-problem cards in the order you will solve them (first 4×50 = 200 sold, then 320 − 200), adding more cards only if a longer problem needs them
Before computing, state 'about how big' the answer should be — set an estimate benchmark (e.g. 'about 300 sold... no, 200, so a bit over 100 left')
Solve each sub-step in order, keeping the whole plan visible

After you have an answer, work backwards through the story (inverse) to see whether you return to the starting number: put back the pencils that were sold, 120 + 4×50 = 120 + 200 = 320. Undo the actions in the problem, not just your own calculation, because undoing a wrong calculation (e.g. 320 − 50 = 270, then 270 + 50 = 320) would still get you back to 320
Compare your answer against your own estimate: if it is wildly off, treat that as a signal to recheck both the answer and the estimate
If an approach stalls, deliberately re-represent the problem a different way — for example switch between a strip/bar diagram and a number line that sequences the jumps — rather than stopping
activities.insight: Decomposition is something you physically arrange and sequence, not a rule triggered by a cue word; the estimate and a backwards check that undoes the problem's actions (not merely the child's own calculation) are two separate signals that can catch a wrong-order or wrong-operation answer.

activities.title: Think-aloud study partner for self-monitoring
steps: Work with a partner (or in-role coach) who never hands over the steps but asks you to state a plan and an estimate before computing
Use a monitoring prompt list to pace yourself through the sub-steps: plan → do a step → check → next
Answer monitoring questions aloud: 'What have you found so far? What's still unknown? How could you check that?'
Justify the order you chose for the sub-steps and explain your reasonableness check in your own words
When you are stuck, respond to the prompt to represent the problem a different way — for example a number line for the sequence of jumps — instead of being given the answer
activities.insight: Self-questioning across sub-steps is a repeatable routine for monitoring progress and catching errors, and being able to explain the sequence and the check shows understanding of the structure.

activities.title: Worked-example reference with revealed self-questions
steps: Study a worked multi-step problem where each sub-step can be revealed one at a time
For each revealed sub-step, read the self-question the solver asked and see why the estimate rules certain answers out
After studying, re-solve a fresh but similar problem yourself, sequencing the steps and doing your own check
activities.insight: Seeing the decomposition and the reasonableness reasoning laid out gives a model of what good monitoring looks like before you do it independently.

activities.title: Reasonableness and wrong-order spotting items
steps: Given a problem and several candidate answers, decide 'which of these answers is impossible, and why?' using estimation
Examine two worked solutions and 'spot the wrong-order calculation' — identify where operations were applied in the wrong sequence

Reason about a realistic item: 'A runner's best time for 100 m is 20 seconds. How long for 1 km?' — explain why it will be more than 10× the 100 m time (tiring over the longer distance), rather than multiplying blindly
activities.insight: Estimation and attention to the real situation let you reject answers that cannot make sense, even before checking the full computation.

checkQuestion: Give a two-step problem within 1000, e.g. 'A shop had 320 pencils. It sold 4 boxes of 50. How many pencils are left?' Before any answer ask: 'How would you break this into parts? About how big should the answer be? Once you have it, how could you check it a different way?' Then discuss what they did — you are surfacing how they plan, estimate and check, not marking the number.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who decomposes it (first 4×50 = 200 sold, then 320 − 200), estimates ('about 300 sold... no, 200, so a bit over 100 left'), gets 120, and checks by a different method or inverse (120 + 200 = 320). The decomposition, the estimate benchmark, and a genuine check are the targets.
